It is not *&ldquo;which commits touched this thing&rdquo;* and it is not *&ldquo;which commits added an entry here&rdquo;*. **So any edit that leaves the count unchanged is INVISIBLE to it**, and the output is a short list rather than an error &mdash; which reads exactly like a complete one. **REPRODUCED ON A REAL QUESTION, NOT A CONSTRUCTED ONE:** `git log -S SELF_EXCLUDED -- tools/cross_tenant_isolation_scope.py` returns **ONE** commit (`c44c5bf2`). The shared registry at `~/SAIRN-SESSION-LOCKS/status/<session>.json` carries exactly **one** `note` string per session, and passing `--note` on a `set` **overwrites it whole** &mdash; no append, no diff, no confirmation, no warning. **MEASURED: two notes addressed to other sessions were destroyed and restored from memory rather than from the tool.** **THE CORRECTION MATTERS MORE THAN THE BUG, and it is recorded rather than quietly fixed:** the first account of this said *a `set` that only meant to change `--state` to `idle` takes the note with it*. **THAT IS FALSE.** `tools/sairn_status.py:351` reads `args.note if args.note is not None else prev.get('note')`, so every unpassed field is CARRIED FORWARD and a bare `set --state idle` preserves the note. **Driven against a scratch registry via `SAIRN_STATUS_DIR` rather than read off the line:** write NOTE ONE &rarr; `set --state idle` &rarr; **NOTE ONE survives** &rarr; `--note "NOTE TWO"` &rarr; NOTE TWO, NOTE ONE gone. A register entry naming the wrong mechanism sends the next session to the wrong line. **WHY THE REAL DEFECT IS STILL WORTH A BUCKET ENTRY:** CLAUDE.md sends every session to this registry FIRST, ahead of the claim record and the open-work index, because it is current without a fetch. It is the platform&rsquo;s fastest cross-session channel and the one with **no durability and no audit** &mdash; a note meant for another session can be gone before that session reads it, **silently at both ends**: the writer sees a normal success line and the reader sees a well-formed row that simply does not contain what was sent. This is a **behaviour change to a SHARED coordination tool**, so it goes to Michael before any code moves. **THE HABIT UNTIL THEN:** anything meant for another session goes in the open-work index **as well as** the note, and after every write print the row back and check each marker is present rather than trusting the write. **A CHANNEL THAT CAN BE SILENTLY OVERWRITTEN IS NOT A DELIVERY MECHANISM** &mdash; and **the write is RE-READ FROM DISK**, the stored text confirmed and echoed back, with a mismatch reported as **exit 2 COULD NOT RUN** rather than a quiet pass &mdash; *&ldquo;it exited 0&rdquo;* and *&ldquo;it stored what I sent&rdquo;* were two claims and only one was being checked. **NOTHING IS EVER DROPPED TO CONTROL GROWTH:** a cap discarding the oldest entries would be the same silent destruction one layer down, so an oversized note **WARNS** the author to prune and keeps every byte. **THE FIRST ENTRY IS DELIBERATELY UNSTAMPED** (arm 13k2): `report()` prints `note[:100]`, so leading every single-entry note with a 40-character header would spend 40% of every preview on a time the row&rsquo;s own `updated` field already carries exactly &mdash; Against the unrelated failures above it matches NONE of the four in either control; against a real mutation it matches that arm and not its neighbour. **THE `(?:)` IS LOAD-BEARING AND I GOT IT WRONG FIRST:** without the group, `FAIL[^\n]*a&#124;b&#124;c` is a top-level alternation and the trailing branches match anywhere, which reported three of four as still matching &mdash; a checker failing for a reason that was about the checker, while checking for exactly that. **A SECOND, NARROWER DEFECT IN ONE OF THEM:** the billing-codes control's expects SHARE alternatives &mdash; m1 is `/falls back to the constant&#124;never ""&#124;real code/` and m3 is `/select is filled&#124;never ""&#124;real code/`, two of three identical &mdash; so M1 and M3 each satisfy the other's pattern and **no anchoring can separate them**. Measured: M1 fails 2 arms and matches m1+m3; M3 fails 2 arms and matches m1+m2+m3. So item 35 is not "make it tamper-evident", it is **close the one hole the grant leaves**. **AND THE OBVIOUS IMPLEMENTATION IS THE WRONG ONE, which is the finding worth having before anyone builds it.** A per-row chain needs the previous row&rsquo;s hash, so it puts a READ on a path whose stated contract is that it must never block and whose 7 callers all ignore its return value &mdash; and worse, **two concurrent writes read the same previous hash and FORK the chain, and with no UPDATE grant NOTHING CAN REPAIR THE FORK.** Every verification from that moment reports a broken chain. No read-before-write, no cost on the hot path, `api/_lib/audit.js` does not change at all, and no fork &mdash; the window is closed before it is hashed. Residual stated rather than hidden: an insertion into the current, not-yet-closed window is invisible until that window closes, bounded by the cadence. **AND WHAT NO CHAIN CAN DO HERE:** direct database access can rewrite rows and recompute the whole chain over them; detection only binds someone limited to the API. **NEXT ACTION.** 35a the checkpoint schema, INSERT+SELECT only, S. 35b the checkpointer on a cadence, M. 35c **the verifier, which is the half that makes the rest real**, M. 35d a control that plants a backdated INSERT into a checkpointed window and demands the verifier find it, plus the other direction, S. **35c and 35d are not optional extras** &mdash; 35a and 35b alone produce a tamper-evident log nobody has ever seen detect tampering, the state `checkblocks.py` sat in for months while always exiting 0. **ONE DECISION FOR MICHAEL FIRST AND IT IS NOT TECHNICAL:** the cadence, and **who reads the verifier&rsquo;s answer**. A detector with no named reader is the `console.warn` problem one layer up, which item 39 just found in the clinic that would never read it. **NOT CLAIMED:** no live tampering is alleged or was looked for &mdash; nothing in any production audit table was read, and the INSERT hole is derived from the grant and the writer | M |

It also sends `is_demo:false`, which is exactly why the bypass mattered and why it had **no AI cost control at all** until today. **Recommended: it stops calling `/api/claude` and gets `api/sairncash/ai.js`, verifying the Stripe subscription server-side then calling `callAnthropic()` in-process** — not a new pattern, it is what `api/law-auth.js:596` and `api/sc-ai.js:259` already do. (2) Decide whether any app should ship a guard that makes this unreachable — the Access panel added in `ce8193e` would have PREVENTED it by surfacing the server's `LAST_OWNER` refusal, but nothing stops the same state being created through the API directly<br><br>**NOT A ONE-OFF — CONFIRMED AS A PATTERN ACROSS FOUR OF THE FIVE APPS, 2026-08-28.** CC raised this while auditing tonight's auth builds and I verified it independently against the source rather than accepting it: `PROVISIONING_ROLES` is a SINGLE role in **SAIRNdental** `['owner']`, **SAIRNmechanical** `['owner']`, **SAIRNroofing** `['owner']` and **SAIRNcode** `['admin']`. Only **StoneDesk** has two, `['owner','admin']`. For all four single-role apps the `setup` gate is bound to that *same* role, so there is genuinely no second path back — RF-PINNACLE-2026 is simply the one where it has already fired. **ONE REFINEMENT TO CC'S FRAMING, worth stating precisely: StoneDesk's exposure is REDUCED, not absent.** Two provisioning roles mean an `admin` can restore a deactivated `owner` and vice versa, so it takes two deactivations rather than one — but if the last active `owner` AND the last active `admin` both go inactive, StoneDesk is locked out identically. The guard question is therefore "how many provisioning-role holders must remain active", not "does this app have two roles". **ONE MORE THING THE COUNT HIDES, verified from source 2026-08-28 (Hank): THE EXISTING GUARD IS PRESENT IN ALL FIVE AND IS PREVENTIVE-ONLY.** Every one of `dnt`, `mech`, `rf`, `sc` and `sd` already carries the last-one refusal — an `activeOwners`/`activeAdmins` `.length <= 1` check before allowing a deactivation. So the exposure is **not a missing guard, it is a missing RECOVERY PATH**: the refusal stops the last active provisioner being deactivated *through* `set_active`, and can do nothing about one that is already inactive — which is exactly how RF-PINNACLE-2026 got here, via verification passes that left rows `active:false` rather than via a refused call. **Consequence for the fix: a harder guard on the deactivation path would not have prevented this and will not prevent the next one.** The two halves are separable and only the second is unsolved — widening the pool (StoneDesk demonstrates it) versus providing a way back (nothing demonstrates it). **AND THE CONCRETE TRAP FOR WHOEVER BUILDS IT: SAIRNcode’s single role is `admin`, not `owner`.** Four of the five say `owner`; `sc-auth.js` says `admin`. A recovery path that names a role instead of reading `PROVISIONING_ROLES` misses SAIRNcode **silently** — the app answers normally right up until someone needs to recover. Scope note: exactly **5 of 16** auth files implement `set_active` at all; the other eleven have neither it nor a `PROVISIONING_ROLES` constant, so they are out of scope rather than unaudited. **This is the input to the harder-guard decision** (action 2 above), and it changes its scope: a fix aimed at one app would leave three with the same exposure. Candidate shapes, none chosen: refuse the deactivation that would take active provisioning-role holders to zero (the `LAST_OWNER` guard already exists but is unreachable by construction — see `sairn-employee-auth-scaffold` §7); or add a break-glass path; or widen `PROVISIONING_ROLES` per app, which is a real authorisation change and not a safety patch | M |
| **Platform** | ~~The seed push gate reads seed files from the **working tree**, not from the commits being pushed~~ | **FIXED 2026-09-03 (Hank)** — 38/38 probe, 9/9 negative controls | Hank | — | `tools/sairn_push_gate_hook.py` calls `tools/sairn_load_state_check.py`, which reads `sql/*.json` **off disk**. So the drift it reports describes HEAD's working tree, not the refspec. **Reproduced, not theorised:** pushing `b351b49` — an engine-only commit touching zero seed files — was DENIED naming 13 missing New Hampshire rules, because the *later* seed commit was sitting in HEAD. This is the exact ordering the gate doc itself prescribes (deploy the computation standard, then load, then push the seed), so **the gate currently denies the workflow it documents.** Fix shape, not chosen: derive the seed set from `git diff` over the pushed range rather than from disk — but note that the disk read is also what makes the check honest about what will be live, so the two readings need reconciling rather than one replacing the other. **Workaround that is not a bypass, and should be preferred to the override:** check out the engine commit detached and push from there — at that commit no seed exists on disk, live genuinely matches repo, and the gate passes on its own terms | S |
| **Platform** | ~~`SAIRN_SEED_GATE=off`, the gate's own documented override, is **unreachable from any Bash tool call**~~ | **FIXED 2026-09-03 (Hank)** — the inline prefix now works; a quoted mention still does not | Hank | — | `tools/sairn_push_gate_hook.py:287` reads `os.environ.get('SAIRN_SEED_GATE')` — the hook runs as a PreToolUse hook inside **Claude Code's** process, so it inherits Claude Code's environment, not the shell's. Prefixing `SAIRN_SEED_GATE=off git push ...` sets the variable in a child shell the hook never sees; it was tried and the push was denied identically. The override therefore only works if it is set in the environment Claude Code itself was launched with, which is not what CLAUDE.md's push protocol describes and not what the denial message tells the reader to do. **Consequence worth stating: the escape hatch every other gate here relies on does not exist for this one in practice**, so a session that hits a false denial has no documented way out. Fix shape, not chosen: read the override out of the hook's `tool_input.command` string (the same payload it already parses for the push refspec) so an inline prefix works, and correct the denial message either way. Related to the row above — they were found together and the working-tree bug is what makes this one bite | S |
